title: Understanding Strain Localization in Magnesium Alloy AZ31 and ZEK100 Through High-Resolution Digital Image Correlation (HRDIC) and Simulation
abstract: Abstract High-resolution digital image correlation (HRDIC) has been used to compare strain localization in conventional AZ31 and dilute rare-earth containing commercial ZEK100 magnesium alloys. The materials were processed to obtain a similar grain structure but have a different texture. It is demonstrated that whilst both alloys show strong concentration of strain in grain boundary regions, this is much more intense in AZ31 than ZEK100. Basal slip is observed to dominate in both AZ31 and ZEK100, although non-basal modes are also more active in the later case. Crystal plasticity simulations have been used to help explain the results. The predictions suggest that the higher local strains observed in AZ31 compared to ZEK100 can be reproduced through the texture difference between the materials alone, at least at the low plastic strains studied here. Other differences between the alloys, such as the ease of activating non-basal slip or grain boundary segregation, are expected but are therefore not essential to produce the difference in strain localization behaviour. These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the improved formability of ZEK100 compared to AZ31 is predominantly a texture effect.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Magnesium alloy sheet is a candidate as a lightweight and recyclable option for mass critical applications such as transportation. A key challenge in shaping magnesium alloy sheet is its poor formability compared to competitor materials. This is fundamentally related to its hexagonal close-packed crystal structure and the resultant deformation mechanisms. However, some magnesium alloys are known to be far more formable than others. For example, alloys such as ZEK100, which contain rare-earth (RE) additions in low concentration, show far greater ductility and formability than conventional RE-free alloys such as AZ31. [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]  The origin of this difference in behaviour has been studied extensively, with a difference in texture playing an important role. [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]  However, in understanding formability, it is necessary to consider not only the global material microstructure and behaviour, but also the local response. Failure in forming initiates at sites of strain localization, so knowledge about the distribution of strain is an important part of understanding performance differences.

High-resolution digital image correlation (HRDIC) offers a technique for mapping local strain distributions and identifying sites of strain concentration. Recent developments in HRDIC as applied to magnesium alloys are now able to obtain a spatial resolution of around 40 nm and a strain resolution of better than 1 pct. [ 4 ]  This is sufficient to resolve individual slip bands, fine twins, and strain localization in grain boundary regions in magnesium alloys. [ 4 , 5 ]  HRDIC has been used to investigate local strain distribution in Mg–Al alloys (AZ31) [ 4 ]  and in concentrated RE containing Mg alloys. [ 6 , 7 ]  However, this technique has not yet been applied to explore the difference in behaviour in dilute Mg–RE alloys ( e.g.  ZEK100) and their non-RE counterparts ( e.g.  AZ31).

Previous HRDIC work has confirmed the highly heterogeneous distribution of strain that develops during deformation of non-RE containing magnesium alloys. Strain is strongly localised at slip bands, twins, and in grain boundary regions. Within grain boundary regions, local axial strains can exceed 30 times the macroscopically imposed strain. [ 4 ]  The nature of the slip bands depends strongly on the active slip system. For example, basal slip in AZ31 usually leads to well-defined, planar slip bands. Non-basal slip produces diffuse and wavy slip bands. [ 4 ]

HRDIC has been used to compare deformation behaviour in AZ31 and binary RE containing alloy Mg–3.5 wt pct Y. [ 7 ]  Regions of intense strain localization were observed in both alloys, particularly in grain boundary regions. The maximum local strains measured in the RE containing alloy were only half that of the RE-free AZ31. In both alloys, basal slip was seen to be the dominant deformation mode. Due to the processing conditions and loading direction, very little twinning was observed and no measurable segregation of Y to the grain boundaries was detected. [ 7 ]  The difference in strain localization was explained in terms of the ease with which slip from one grain could trigger slip in its neighbour, which was characterised depending on boundary misorientation. The difference in misorientation distribution between AZ31 and Mg–3.5 wt pct Y (which results from the texture difference between alloys) was identified as the main cause for reduced strain localization in the latter case. It should be noted that the RE content of this alloy is over 10 times that of ZEK100, so the applicability of these findings to dilute RE alloys remains a knowledge gap to be addressed here.

Binary magnesium alloys with other RE additions have also been studied. Mg–3 wt pct Er and Mg–3 wt pct Dy alloys were compressed  in situ  and analysed  via  EBSD and electron channelling contrast imaging (ECCI). [ 8 ]  These techniques do not directly measure deformation in the way HRDIC does, but instead can indirectly capture strain through measurement of the geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). Basal slip and twinning were found to be the dominant deformation modes in all cases. The role of basal slip percolation between grains in establishing persistent shear bands was identified. Crystal plasticity simulations were used to interpret the results. [ 8 ]

The grain-scale tensile deformation of an alloy with a dilute RE content closer to that of ZEK100 (Mg–0.8 wt pct Y) has been investigated using surface analysis of slip traces. [ 9 ]  No HRDIC was performed, so the local strain distribution was not studied. Despite an apparently unfavourable near basal texture, basal slip was shown to be the dominant deformation mode. Crystal plasticity modelling was applied and correctly predicted this observation. [ 9 ]

Dilute RE containing alloys with other additions (Zn, which is also present in ZEK100 and Ca which is not) have also been studied and compared with a matched binary RE alloy (Mg–0.6 wt pct Gd) using slip trace analysis. [ 10 ]  Basal slip was seen to be the dominant deformation mode in all cases. The alloy with Zn and Ca additions exhibited increased ductility. This was attributed to enhanced basal slip, suppression of slip localization through increased frequency of grain boundaries disoriented favourably for slip transfer, and increased grain boundary cohesion. [ 10 ]

Strain localization has been related to the ease with which slip in one grain can trigger slip in its neighbour. [ 7 , 11 ]  Where this is easy, the accumulation of local strain in the grain boundary regions is reduced, which has been associated with an increase in ductility. [ 7 , 10 ]  On the other hand, transfer of slip (or twins) from one grain to the next can trigger a chain of slip or twining bands across the polycrystal that then produce macroscopic strain localization leading to failure. [ 11 , 12 ]

Experiments suggest that in magnesium, grain boundaries with disorientations below approximately 40 deg facilitate slip in one grain triggering slip in its neighbour. [ 7 , 10 ]  High-resolution crystal plasticity modelling work that explicitly captures slip banding in a bi-crystal demonstrates that whilst the disorientation across the boundary is important, the tendency for slip band transmission is most dependent on the stress at the slip band tip. [ 11 ]  The model also demonstrates that for low disorientation angles, slip in one grain is likely to lead to slip of the same type in its neighbour.

sections.heading: Experimental Method
paragraphs: Dog-bone shaped tensile samples were prepared for deformation and HRDIC study by electrical discharge machining. Small specimens are required to fit within the scanning electron microscope (SEM) for analysis. The specimens had a gauge length of 26 mm and width of 5 mm. Grip sections were 10.15 mm long and 10 mm wide. The total specimen length was 53 mm, with fillets of 3.5 mm radius to connect the gauge and grip regions. Specimens were cut with their long axes parallel to rolling direction (RD) of the sheet.

Identification of slip bands measured in the HRDIC strain maps was performed by correlating against EBSD crystallographic data using the capabilities within the DefDAP software package. [ 13 ]  The relative displacement ratio (RDR) method [ 17 ]  was used to classify the slip bands. This method works well for the sharp slip bands, typical of basal slip. A confidence level > 0.9 was set as the threshold for assigning an observed slip band to a particular slip system. Using this criterion, it was not possible to unambiguously identify some of the diffuse and wavy slip features seen in the strain maps and this will be discussed later.

sections.heading: Crystal Plasticity Simulation
paragraphs: Spatially resolved crystal plasticity models can provide a useful comparison to experimental HRDIC data. They allow the extent of strain localization to be predicted based on the material texture and grain structure. Importantly, the crystal plasticity model enables the effect of texture and CRSS differences to be decoupled in a way that is not possible experimentally.

The DAMASK crystal plasticity framework was used to perform simulations of the strain distribution obtained after tensile testing in the present work. Details of this model, and its application to magnesium alloys, are given elsewhere. [ 8 , 18 , 19 ]  The same methodology was followed here, with the single-crystal behaviour being captured using the phenomenological crystal plasticity model described in Reference [ 18 ]. Single-crystal parameters for AZ31 were initially taken from Reference [ 18 , 19 ] and for ZEK100 from Reference [ 20 ]. However, it was not possible to fit the experimental stress–strain curves using these values; in particular, the flow stress of AZ31 was significantly underestimated. Therefore, a refinement of critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) values was performed to give reasonable agreement with the experimental flow stress curves. This involved increasing the CRSS values for basal and non-basal slip in AZ31 compared to those reported in Reference [ 18 ].

It is important to note that whilst the CP model used here is spatially resolved (unlike self-consistent models such as VPSC [ 21 , 22 ] ), its resolution is not sufficient to capture individual slip bands. This means that in the CP model, strain localization arises only from the grain geometry and texture, and transfer of deformation from one grain to its neighbour arises from averaged stresses not individual slip bands.

The model components were integrated into a single workflow  via  the Matflow package. [ 23 ]  The simulation was run at a nominal strain rate to match the experimental tensile test, and 200 simulation steps were used for a total strain of 6.5 pct. This was found to be the maximum strain level for which the model reliably ran for both alloys and exceeds the 2 pct strain imposed in the HRDIC tests.

sections.heading: Experimental Results
paragraphs: As expected, there is a significant difference in texture between the two alloys. AZ31 shows a strong basal texture, with a maximum intensity of 6.4 times that of a random distribution (MRD = 6.4). Figure  1  shows that although most grains are in a basal orientation (red), there are a small number of grains in prismatic or other orientations. Fig. 1 ( a ) EBSD map of AZ31 after heat treatment. ( b ) Pole figures showing the strong basal texture Fig. 2 ( a ) EBSD map of ZEK100 after heat treatment. ( b ) Pole figures showing the weaker texture with a basal pole split in the transverse direction Fig. 3 Grain size distributions for AZ31 and ZEK100 showing evidence of a bimodal distribution in ZEK100

The texture of ZEK100 is weaker overall with a spread of basal poles towards the transverse direction (TD). The maximum intensity is 4.5 times that of a random distribution (MRD = 4.5). The TD basal pole split is typical of dilute RE magnesium sheet. [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]

The gold remodelling process was successful and micrographs showing the gold speckle pattern on the surface of both alloys are presented in Figure  4 . The average speckle size was 40 nm in both cases. Fig. 4 Gold speckle pattern on ( a ) AZ31 and ( b ) ZEK100. The average speckle size is 40 nm in both cases

Strain concentration is observed at certain grain boundaries and in sharply defined slip bands within some grains, the latter being especially prominent in AZ31. The maximum local equivalent shear strain in AZ31 is 0.8 evidencing very strong localization. This is also significantly greater than the maximum local shear strain measured in ZEK100, which is 0.5. The point of maximum strain is labelled ‘Max’. In both cases, the highest local shear strain is within a grain boundary region whose trace at the surface is inclined close to 45 deg to the loading direction.

For AZ31, the region of maximum shear strain can be seen to be part of a larger feature of high strain concentration which traverses from the bottom left to top right of the image, following grain boundaries or twins and inclined to the loading direction. In ZEK100, the regions of high strain also encompass multiple grain boundaries, but are isolated from each other by lower strain regions. Fig. 6 Low-magnification HRDIC derived maps of equivalent plastic strain for ( a ) AZ31 and ( b ) ZEK100. Regions of maximum strain localization with the effective strain level, example twins, sharp planar slip bands, and diffuse strain (slip) are indicated

Histograms showing the local effective shear strain distribution are presented in Figure  7 . The complete histogram for both alloys is shown in Figure  7 (a), with a rescaled version focussing on the high strain tail in Figure  7 (b). The histograms confirm the qualitative observations from the maps showing that AZ31 has a higher occurrence of high strain concentration than ZEK100. The upper decile local equivalent shear strain for AZ31 is 0.256, which is approximately 10 times greater than that for ZEK100, which is 0.022. The upper quartile values are 0.090 and 0.014 for AZ31 and ZEK100, respectively. In both cases, this is consistent with the observation of a long tail corresponding to regions of very high strain localization in AZ31. Fig. 7 Histograms showing the local effective shear strain distribution for AZ31 and ZEK100 ( a ) full range, and ( b ) rescaled to show the high strain tail

Higher magnification images showing particular regions of intense strain localization are presented in Figure  8  for AZ31 and ZEK100. These regions of strain localization correspond mainly to grain boundaries (GBs) but highly concentrated strain can also be seen in slip bands; this is particularly noteworthy in Figure  8 (b) for AZ31, labelled SB.

Localization in grain boundary regions usually occurs when the grain boundary trace is inclined to the loading direction (RD). However, in some cases, grain boundaries whose trace at the surface is near perpendicular to the loading direction also show high local strain, an example being given in Figure  8 (f). It is possible here that the grain boundary is similarly inclined to the loading direction, but in the through thickness direction, which cannot be seen in this 2-dimensional analysis.

Grain pairs were also observed where slip in one grain appeared to have triggered slip in the neighbouring grain, with matching slip bands observed on either side of the grain boundary. Example cases are presented in Figure  9  for AZ31 and ZEK100. Grain boundary positions were extracted from the EBSD data and shown as thick white lines in this figure.

Grain pairs where a slip band in one grain most readily produces a matching slip band in the neighbouring grain were observed when the disorientation between the grains is small [for the examples shown, the angle between the basal slip bands is 27 deg in (a) and 12 deg in (b)]. Fig. 9 Examples of grain pairs showing evidence of slip in one grain triggering slip in a neighbouring grain, with matching slip bands on either side of a grain boundary indicated by arrows ( a ) AZ31, and ( b ) ZEK100

As demonstrated, strong planar slip bands are observed in some grains for both alloys. In addition, evidence of diffuse slip is also seen, particularly in ZEK100. Given the expected importance of basal slip, it is useful to plot the orientation EBSD data in terms of the Schmid Factor (SF) for basal slip activation where the tensile axis is the reference direction. EBSD maps plotted this way are shown in Figure  10 . This demonstrates that whilst the overall texture of AZ31 is significantly different from that of ZEK100, most grains in both alloys are tilted away from the ideal basal orientation enough to give a SF that is suﬃcient to allow activation of basal slip (SF > 0.1 in pure magnesium [ 25 ] ). Fig. 10 Crystal orientations plotted as Schmid factor for basal slip for ( a ) AZ31 and ( b ) ZEK100

Slip trace analysis was performed by correlating EBSD and HRDIC data using the RDR method. [ 17 ]  Examples of slip trace identification for AZ31 are shown in Figure  11  for three grains exhibiting different behaviour. Grain 1 contains sharp, planar slip bands. The orientation of these bands matches well with the basal plane, confirming they correspond to basal slip. Grain 2 shows distinct slip bands that are less sharp (more diffuse) than those seen in grain 1. Slip trace analysis demonstrates that these bands are also closely aligned with the basal plane and therefore also correspond to basal slip activity. This is despite the macroscopic SF for basal slip being only 0.11 in this grain. Grain 3 shows weaker and more diffuse slip bands, with multiple band orientations seen within a single grain. Furthermore, the bands are less planar, showing evidence of some waviness. The alignment of these bands, although difficult to determine precisely, corresponds to a prismatic plane orientation, suggesting they are produced by prismatic slip. The SF for prismatic slip in this grain (0.48) is high, confirming the grain is well oriented for this deformation mode. Fig. 11 Slip trace analysis for AZ31 for 3 example grains demonstrating different behaviour. Grain 1: Sharp planar slip bands. Grain 2: More diffuse planar slip bands. Grain 3: Diffuse slip bands. Exp trace is the measured trace direction, theo traces are the ideal (theoretical) trace directions for the known grain orientation

sections.heading: Simulation Results
paragraphs: Crystal plasticity simulations were used to help interpret the experimental results. First, the ability of the CP model to produce the correct stress–strain behaviour was investigated using CRSS parameters as presented in Table  1 . The calibrated model and experimentally measured stress–strain curves are presented in Figures  13 (a and b). It can be seen that although the model slightly over-estimates the flow strength of AZ31 whilst underestimating that of ZEK100, it predicts behaviour to within 20 MPa of measurement. Model predictions are truncated at 6 pct strain. Beyond this, the predicted strain localization became too large for the model to converge to a solution. Since this strain is much greater than that used in the HRDIC experiment (2 pct), this does not present a problem in the present work.

The initial RVE and final predicted distribution of strain [Von-Mises (VM) equivalent] are shown for AZ31 at 2 pct (0.02) applied strain in Figure  14 . This applied strain level was chosen to match that in the HRDIC study. As with the experiment, regions of high localised strain are predicted, concentrated mainly at grain boundaries. Where the grain boundaries are aligned, these regions of high concentration can be continuous over several grains. The maximum VM equivalent strain was predicted as 0.12. Fig. 14 ( a ) Initial representative volume element (RVE) for AZ31 crystal plasticity simulations. ( b ) Predicted Von-Mises equivalent local strain map after 2 pct macroscopic strain for AZ31

The initial RVE and final predicted distribution of strain are shown for ZEK100 at 2 pct applied strain in Figure  15 . Strain localization is also predicted in this case, mainly concentrated at grain boundaries, but its intensity is significantly less than that for AZ31. The maximum VM equivalent local strain was predicted as 0.074. Fig. 15 ( a ) Initial representative volume element (RVE) for ZEK100 crystal plasticity simulations. ( b ) Von-Mises equivalent local strain map after 2 pct macroscopic strain for ZEK100

The predicted evolution of the strain distribution with increasing applied strain is shown for both alloys in Figure  16 . It can be seen that as the applied strain increases, so does the intensity of strain localization. However, the points where the strongest strain concentration is observed at the highest strain level were also sites of strain concentration at lower strain and this is consistent in both AZ31 and ZEK100. This demonstrates that the strain hot spots are predicted to develop early during deformation and then intensify as applied strain increases. Finally, the simulations confirm that strain localization is always greater in AZ31 than ZEK100 for the same applied strain level. Fig. 16 Predicted evolution of local strain with increasing macroscopic strain (2, 4, and 6 pct) for ( a  through  c ) AZ31 and ( d  through  f ) ZEK100. The dotted line indicates the position used for line profile sampling

A quantitative comparison of the evolution of strain localization was performed by taking line profiles. Figure  17  shows the development of heterogeneity in strain, even at the lowest applied strain levels. All the positions of maximum local strain at the final macroscopic strain (6 pct) were present at the lowest applied strain level (2 pct) so that the predicted effect of increasing the applied strain is to shift and scale the strain distribution rather than introduce new sites of high localization. The line profiles confirm the much greater range of local strains in AZ31 than ZEK100 at all applied strain levels. Fig. 17 Predicted evolution of local strain along a line profile with increasing macroscopic strain (2, 4, and 6 pct) for ( a ) AZ31 and ( b ) ZEK100

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Factors controlling plasticity of a polycrystalline metal include the fundamental single-crystal constitutive properties, the size, shape and distribution of grains, recrystallized fraction, and the crystallographic texture on both local and global scales. As demonstrated in this study, as-received commercially rolled magnesium alloys (AZ31 and ZEK100) are different in all of these parameters, making it difficult to understand which are most important in governing behaviour.

To address this issue, heat treatments were used to produce grain structures that were as similar as possible in both alloys investigated. The differences between the materials are then confined mainly to the single-crystal behaviour, crystallographic texture, and grain boundary characteristics.

Consistent with previous work comparing conventional (non-RE) magnesium sheet (AZ31) and RE containing sheet (ZEK100), a significant texture difference is seen. The texture of ZEK100 is weaker, but also shows a split in basal pole maximum intensity away from the ideal basal texture and towards the transverse direction (TD). [ 3 ]  This texture difference is considered largely responsible for the improved forming performance of ZEK100 compared to AZ31. [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]

Examination of the strain maps produced by HRDIC reveals a heterogeneous distribution of strain in both AZ31 and ZEK100, even after application of only 2 pct macroscopic plastic strain. For AZ31, the maximum local effective shear strain was observed to reach 0.8. This is similar to the maximum local equivalent shear strain of 0.86 observed in a previous HRDIC study of AZ31, deformed to a slightly higher macroscopic strain. [ 4 ]  Strain concentration was also observed in ZEK100 HRDIC maps, but to a lesser extent. The maximum local effective shear strain in this case was observed to reach 0.5. Although significantly lower than the value for AZ31, this demonstrates that a strong concentration of strain also occurs in grain boundary regions for the RE containing alloy.

The ratio of maximum local strain in AZ31 compared to that in ZEK100 is 1.63. This is similar to the equivalent ratio found when comparing AZ31 and binary Mg–3.4 wt pct Y, which was 1.85. [ 7 ]  This suggests that ZEK100 behaves similarly to alloys with a much higher RE content, such as Mg–3.4 wt pct Y when considering strain localization. This is consistent with the understanding that special deformation effects attributed to addition of RE in magnesium alloys are activated at low levels of addition, and further RE does not produce significant further change. [ 26 ]

In both AZ31 and ZEK100, higher magnification inspection of the HRDIC maps reveals many grains in both AZ31 and ZEK100 that contain sharply defined parallel planar slip bands. These bands correspond to basal slip activity. The dominant role of basal slip in the deformation of both alloys for this loading direction is consistent with previous studies. [ 7 , 10 ]  It can also be explained through inspection of the Schmid factor maps (Figure  10 ). These maps demonstrate that although the grains are not well oriented for basal slip in either alloy, there is sufficient deviation from the ideal basal orientation to activate the easy basal mode. [ 25 ]

As in previous HRDIC studies, slip bands in one grain were seen to trigger slip in a neighbouring grain. This tendency was greatest when the disorientation between grains was low. Although quantifying this behaviour was not an aim of this study and a statistical analysis of many grains was not performed, the observations of slip triggering with disorientation angles up to approximately 30 deg are consistent with previous studies. [ 11 , 25 ]

Full-field crystal plasticity simulation has been used to help isolate which of these effects is essential to explain the difference in strain localization observed in AZ31 and ZEK100. The CP model correctly predicts the greater tendency for strain localization in AZ31 compared to ZEK100. It predicts a ratio of maximum local strain in AZ31 that is 1.62 times greater than that in ZEK100. This compares very well with the measured value for this ratio of 1.63. This difference between alloys is clear in the predictions even though the CP model does not capture individual slip bands.

The HRDIC experiment was limited to an applied strain (2 pct) well below the failure strain. However, the simulation suggests that the dominant effect when strain increases is to intensify the sites of strain localization formed at low strain rather than introduce any new sites. Close to the failure point, additional deformation modes and sites of strain localization may occur, especially since the local stress state will be altered by necking. The rare-earth additions may play a role at this near to fracture point in controlling this behaviour. This is a possible additional effect that was not explored in the present study.

The CP model can be used to isolate the effect of texture alone on strain localization by performing a simulation that is not possible by experiment. A prediction was made using the single-crystal properties of AZ31 but with the texture of ZEK100. The results of this simulation at 6 pct macroscopic strain are compared with the previous AZ31 and ZEK100 predictions in Figure  19 . The original simulation for AZ31 (AZ31sx, AZ31tex) is shown in Figure  19 (a). The prediction with the same single-crystal properties (AZ31sx) but the texture of ZEK100 (ZEK100tex) is shown in Figure  19 (b). The local strain distribution can be seen quantitatively in the line profiles (Figure  19 (c)). By swapping the initial texture of AZ31 to that of ZEK100 but keeping the single-crystal properties of AZ31 the maximum local strain is halved from 0.20 to 0.10. This closely matches the maximum local strain for ZEK100 (ZEK100sx–ZEK100tex), which is 0.11. Fig. 19 ( a ) Predicted Von-Mises equivalent local strain map after 6 pct macroscopic strain for AZ31 crystal properties using AZ31 texture. ( b ) Predicted Von-Mises equivalent local strain map after 6 pct macroscopic strain for AZ31 crystal properties using ZEK100 texture. ( c ) Strain distribution along a line parallel to RD

This simulation therefore demonstrates that the texture difference alone between AZ31 and ZEK100 is sufficient to reduce the strain localization in AZ31 to the level seen in ZEK100. Whilst factors such as a difference in single-crystal properties and grain boundary segregation effects are also expected, they are not essential to explain the reduced strain localization in ZEK100.

Other factors such as the grain structure, additional slip and twinning modes, the presence of second phase particles, and grain boundary cohesion will become increasingly important close to failure, but all else being equal, the reduced tendency for strain localization in ZEK100 due to the texture effect alone should lead to improved formability, as observed in practice.

An alternative way of stating this is that if AZ31 were to have the same texture as ZEK100, it is likely to be similarly formable. This is consistent with work that shows non-conventional thermomechanical processing that weakens the strong basal texture of AZ31 significantly improving its formability ( e.g.  Reference [ 30 ]).
